summary.text: Couple the mass-�n+1 evolution to the mass-�n evolution by tracking one extra grain, which stays put or moves one site right according to the parity of the mass beneath it; mass conservation, hole-freeness, and the form \([1^{n-2},2]\) of the unique final predecessor force this grain to be at position \(n-1\) or \(n-2\) when the mass-�n system first stabilizes. Thereafter the stable block of ones makes the grain move right one site per step, and the larger system stabilizes exactly when it reaches position \(n\), hence one or two steps later.

full_proof.text:
For a configuration, it is convenient to append infinitely many zero cells and regard it as a function
\[
 f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N.
\]
Number the cells from left to right starting at position \(0\). Define the one-step operator \(F\) by
\[
 (Ff)(0)=\left\lceil\frac{f(0)}2\right\rceil
       =\frac{f(0)+1}{2},
\]
and, for \(i>0\),
\[
 (Ff)(i)=\left\lceil\frac{f(i)}2\right\rceil
          +\left\lfloor\frac{f(i-1)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
Here and below division in expressions involving integers has the usual floor interpretation. Thus each cell keeps the ceiling of half its mass and receives the floor of half the mass in the cell immediately to its left.

Let \(E_n(t,i)\) be the mass at position \(i\) after \(t\) steps when the initial mass is \(n\) at the origin:
\[
 E_n(0,i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
 \qquad E_n(t+1,\cdot)=F(E_n(t,\cdot)).
\]
Write \(Q_n\) for the stable target configuration
\[
 Q_n(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<n,\\0,&i\ge n.\end{cases}
\]
The target is fixed by \(F\). Indeed, a cell containing \(1\) keeps \(1\) and sends \(0\), while a zero cell remains zero; checking the boundary between positions \(n-1\) and \(n\) gives the same conclusion. Consequently, once \(E_n(t)=Q_n\), this equality persists at all later times.

We first record several basic structural facts about this evolution.

1. Finite support and conservation of mass.

After \(t\) steps, no mass can lie to the right of position \(t\):
\[
 i>t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_n(t,i)=0.
\]
This follows immediately by induction, since mass moves at most one position to the right in one step.

The total mass is always \(n\). One direct finite-sum verification is useful. For any function \(f\) and any \(M\ge0\),
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{M}(Ff)(i)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}f(i)+\left\lceil\frac{f(M)}2\right\rceil.
\]
To see this, expand the left side. Every \(f(i)\) for \(i<M\) contributes
\(\lceil f(i)/2\rceil+\lfloor f(i)/2\rfloor=f(i)\), while at the right boundary only the retained half of \(f(M)\) occurs. If \(f(M)=0\), the boundary term vanishes. Combining this identity with the support bound and inducting on time shows that, whenever \(M>t\),
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{M-1}E_n(t,i)=n. \tag{1}
\]

2. There are no holes in the occupied portion.

Call \(f\) hole-free if
\[
 f(i)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(i+1)=0
\]
for every \(i\). If \(f\) is hole-free, then so is \(Ff\). For example, if \((Ff)(0)=0\), then \(f(0)=0\), hence \(f(1)=0\), and therefore \((Ff)(1)=0\). For \(i>0\), if \((Ff)(i)=0\), both nonnegative summands in
\[
 (Ff)(i)=\left\lceil f(i)/2\right\rceil+\\left\lfloor f(i-1)/2\right\rfloor
\]
vanish. In particular \(f(i)=0\), so hole-freeness gives \(f(i+1)=0\), and then \((Ff)(i+1)=0\). The initial configuration is hole-free, so every \(E_n(t)\) is hole-free. Iterating the defining implication gives the stronger consequence
\[
 E_n(t,i)=0,\ j\ge i\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_n(t,j)=0. \tag{2}
\]

We next couple the evolutions with initial masses \(n\) and \(n+1\).

For a configuration \(f\), let \(f+\delta_s\) denote the result of adding one unit at position \(s\). A direct calculation gives the fundamental one-step coupling identity
\[
 F(f+\delta_s)=Ff+\delta_{s+(f(s)\bmod 2)}. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, if \(f(s)\) is even, adding one changes the retained ceiling half at \(s\) by one and does not change the amount sent right, so the extra unit remains at \(s\). If \(f(s)\) is odd, adding one does not change the retained half but increases the floor half sent to \(s+1\) by one, so the extra unit moves to \(s+1\). All other cells are unchanged.

Define the tracked grain position \(g_n(t)\) by
\[
 g_n(0)=0,
 \qquad
 g_n(t+1)=g_n(t)+\bigl(E_n(t,g_n(t))\bmod 2\bigr). \tag{4}
\]
Starting from the obvious identity between the initial configurations and applying (3) inductively yields
\[
 E_{n+1}(t)=E_n(t)+\delta_{g_n(t)}. \tag{5}
\]
Thus the mass-
\(n+1\) system is exactly the mass-\(n\) system together with one extra grain whose motion is described by (4).

We need two consequences of this coupling.

First, if
\[
 g_n(t)=n, \tag{6}
\]
then \(E_n(t)=Q_n\). To prove this, use (5) and the fact that \(E_{n+1}(t)\) is hole-free. For every \(i<n\), the value \(E_n(t,i)\) must be positive. Otherwise the coupled configuration would also be zero at \(i\), because its extra grain is at \(n\); hole-freeness would then force it to be zero at \(n\), contradicting the presence there of the extra grain. Hence each of the first \(n\) entries of \(E_n(t)\) is at least one. Their sum is therefore at least \(n\), while the total mass is exactly \(n\) by (1). It follows that all these entries equal one and every later entry is zero. This is precisely \(Q_n\).

Second,
\[
 g_n(t)\le n\quad\text{for every }t. \tag{7}
\]
This is an induction. If \(g_n(t)<n\), equation (4) advances the grain by at most one. If \(g_n(t)=n\), the preceding result says that \(E_n(t)=Q_n\), whose value at \(n\) is zero, so the grain does not advance. Thus it never passes \(n\).

We now establish the main invariant controlling the grain. For every \(t\), either the mass-\(n\) system is stable, or there is a cell different from one no farther right than one position beyond the grain:
\[
 E_n(t)=Q_n
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \exists i\le g_n(t)+1\text{ such that }E_n(t,i)\ne1. \tag{8}
\]

We prove (8) by induction on \(t\). At time zero, position \(1\) has value zero and \(1\le g_n(0)+1\), so the second alternative holds. If the system is already stable, it remains stable after a step. It remains to handle the second alternative.

Choose \(p\) to be the least index for which \(E_n(t,p)\ne1\). The witness in (8) ensures
\[
 p\le g_n(t)+1, \tag{9}
\]
and minimality gives
\[
 E_n(t,j)=1\quad(j<p). \tag{10}
\]
There are three cases.

If \(E_n(t,p)=0\), then after one step the value at \(p\) is still zero. If \(p=0\), this is immediate. If \(p>0\), the cell at \(p\) retains zero and the cell at \(p-1\), whose mass is one by (10), sends zero. Thus position \(p\) remains a non-one, and by (9) it is still at most one position beyond the new grain, since the grain never moves left.

Suppose next that \(E_n(t,p)=2\). If \(E_n(t,p+1)=0\), hole-freeness says that all entries from \(p+1\) onward are zero. Hence the whole configuration is
\[
 \underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{p\text{ entries}},2,0,0,\ldots.
\]
Mass conservation gives \(n=p+2\). One more step turns this into \(p+2\) consecutive ones: each initial one stays one, the \(2\) at \(p\) leaves one at \(p\) and sends one to \(p+1\), and everything farther right remains zero. Thus the new configuration is \(Q_n\).

If instead \(E_n(t,p+1)>0\), then after one step position \(p+1\) has value at least two: it receives one from the mass \(2\) at \(p\), in addition to retaining at least one from its own positive mass. We must also check its distance from the grain. If \(g_n(t)\ge p\), then plainly \(p+1\le g_n(t+1)+1\). If \(g_n(t)<p\), (9) forces \(g_n(t)=p-1\). By (10), the mass under the grain is then one, so (4) moves the grain to \(p\). Again \(p+1\le g_n(t+1)+1\). Thus position \(p+1\) supplies the required witness.

Finally, if \(E_n(t,p)\ge3\), then the retained amount at \(p\) after a step is at least two, so position \(p\) remains different from one. Its required distance bound follows from (9) and the fact that the grain does not move left. These cases prove (8).

The next ingredient classifies the last nonstable configuration before stabilization.

Assume \(n\ge2\),
\[
 E_n(t+1)=Q_n,
 \qquad E_n(t)\ne Q_n. \tag{11}
\]
Then necessarily
\[
 E_n(t,i)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&i<n-2,\\
 2,&i=n-2,\\
 0,&i>n-2.
 \end{cases} \tag{12}
\]

To prove this, choose the least \(k\) such that \(E_n(t,k)\ne1\). Such a \(k\) exists because the configuration has finite support. We first have \(k<n\): if all positions below \(n\) were one, their total mass would already be \(n\), so conservation would force all later entries to be zero, making the configuration \(Q_n\), contrary to (11).

The value at \(k\) cannot be zero. If it were, hole-freeness would make every entry from \(k\) onward zero, while all earlier entries are one. The total mass would then be \(k<n\), contradicting conservation. Hence
\[
 E_n(t,k)\ge2. \tag{13}
\]
Also \(k+1<n\). Otherwise \(k=n-1\); but the mass at \(k\), being at least two, would send at least one unit to position \(n\), whereas the target \(Q_n\) has value zero there.

Since position \(k\) is inside the target, its value after the step is one. The contribution from the left is zero: if \(k>0\), the preceding value is one, and a cell of mass one sends zero. Thus
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{E_n(t,k)}2\right\rceil=1.
\]
Together with (13), this forces \(E_n(t,k)=2\). At position \(k+1\), the target value is also one, and it receives exactly one from the \(2\) at \(k\). Consequently it must retain zero of its own mass, so \(E_n(t,k+1)=0\). Hole-freeness now makes every position at least \(k+1\) zero. The total mass is therefore
\[
 k\cdot1+2=k+2,
\]
so conservation gives \(n=k+2\), or \(k=n-2\). This proves (12).

We can now locate the tracked grain at the exact stabilization time. Let
\[
 T_n=\min\{t:E_n(t)=Q_n\},
\]
provided this set is nonempty. We shall simultaneously prove that such a time exists for every \(n\ge1\), and that
\[
 T_{n+1}-T_n\in\{1,2\}.
\]
The base case is \(n=1\): the initial configuration is already \(Q_1\), so \(T_1=0\).

Fix \(n\ge1\) and suppose \(T=T_n\) exists. We claim that at time \(T\),
\[
 g_n(T)=n-1\quad\text{or}\quad g_n(T)=n-2, \tag{14}
\]
where for \(n=1\) only the first alternative is relevant. For \(n=1\), \(T=0\) and \(g_1(0)=0=n-1\).

Now suppose \(n\ge2\). Then \(T>0\), because at time zero position \(1<n\) is zero. Write \(T=u+1\). By minimality of \(T\), the configuration at time \(u\) is nonstable, while that at time \(u+1\) is stable. The predecessor classification (12) says that at time \(u\) the entries below \(n-2\) are one, the entry at \(n-2\) is two, and every later entry is zero.

The grain cannot satisfy \(g_n(u)=n\), because that would force the underlying mass-\(n\) system to be stable, as proved above. On the other hand, invariant (8) supplies a non-one position \(i\le g_n(u)+1\). In the predecessor configuration every position below \(n-2\) is one, so \(i\ge n-2\). Therefore
\[
 n-2\le g_n(u)+1.
\]
Together with \(g_n(u)<n\), this leaves only the three possibilities
\[
 g_n(u)=n-1,\quad n-2,\quad\text{or }n-3
\]
(omitting any impossible negative-index case for small \(n\)). We apply the grain update (4) in each case:

* If \(g_n(u)=n-1\), the mass under it is zero, so it stays at \(n-1\).
* If \(g_n(u)=n-2\), the mass under it is two, which is even, so it stays at \(n-2\).
* If \(g_n(u)=n-3\), the mass under it is one, so it moves to \(n-2\).

Thus at time \(T=u+1\) the grain is indeed at \(n-1\) or \(n-2\), proving (14).

From time \(T\) onward, the underlying configuration remains \(Q_n\). As long as the grain is at a position below \(n\), it therefore sits on a cell of mass one. Equation (4) then moves it exactly one place to the right at each step. Hence, for every \(j\) up to the time it reaches \(n\),
\[
 E_n(T+j)=Q_n,
 \qquad
 g_n(T+j)=g_n(T)+j. \tag{15}
\]
By (14), the required number
\[
 j_0=n-g_n(T)

automatically belongs to \(\{1,2\}\). At time \(T+j_0\), the underlying system is stable and the grain is at \(n\).

It remains to relate this to stabilization of the mass-\(n+1\) system and to verify minimality. The precise characterization is
\[
 E_{n+1}(v)=Q_{n+1}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E_n(v)=Q_n\ \text{ and }\ g_n(v)=n. \tag{16}
\]

For the reverse implication, simply add a unit at position \(n\) to \(Q_n\); the result is \(Q_{n+1}\), and (5) then proves the claim.

For the forward implication, suppose the left side of (16) holds, and put \(s=g_n(v)\). We know \(s\le n\) from (7). Evaluating (5) at \(s\), where \(Q_{n+1}\) has value one, shows that \(E_n(v,s)=0\), because the extra grain itself contributes the full unit. If \(s<n\), evaluating (5) at position \(n\) would give \(E_n(v,n)=1\), since the extra grain is not there and \(Q_{n+1}(n)=1\). But hole-freeness, starting from the zero at \(s<n\), would force \(E_n(v,n)=0\), a contradiction. Therefore \(s=n\). As shown earlier, grain position \(n\) forces \(E_n(v)=Q_n\). This proves (16).

Using (15) and (16), the mass-\(n+1\) system is stable at \(T+j_0\). It cannot be stable earlier. If \(v<T\), the mass-\(n\) system is not yet stable, so (16) excludes stability of the mass-\(n+1\) system. If \(T\le v<T+j_0\), write \(v=T+j\). Then (15) gives
\[
 g_n(v)=g_n(T)+j<n,
\]
so (16) again excludes stability. Consequently
\[
 T_{n+1}=T_n+j_0,
 \qquad j_0\in\{1,2\}. \tag{17}
\]
In particular, existence of \(T_n\) implies existence of \(T_{n+1}\). Starting from \(T_1=0\), induction proves existence for every positive \(n\), and (17) proves the desired one-or-two increment for these function-valued configurations.

Finally, we identify this stabilization time with the sequence \(a(n)\) as defined using finite lists and deletion of trailing zeros.

Given a finite list \(L=(L_0,\ldots,L_{r-1})\), extend it by zeros to a function
\[
 \widehat L(i)=\begin{cases}L_i,&i<r,\\0,&i\ge r.\end{cases}
\]
The finite-list update first forms the retained masses
\[
 \left(\left\lceil L_0/2\right\rceil,\ldots,
       \left\lceil L_{r-1}/2\right\rceil,0\right)
\]
and the received masses
\[
 \left(0,\left\lfloor L_0/2\right\rfloor,\ldots,
       \left\lfloor L_{r-1}/2\right\rfloor\right),
\]
adds them coordinatewise, and deletes all trailing zeros. Deleting trailing zeros does not change the zero-extended function. Coordinate by coordinate, the zero extension of this updated list is therefore exactly \(F(\widehat L)\). Induction on time shows that if \(L_n(t)\) is the list obtained after \(t\) updates from \([n]\), then
\[
 \widehat{L_n(t)}(i)=E_n(t,i) \quad\text{for every }i. \tag{18}
\]

For \(n>0\), the initial list has no trailing zero, and every subsequent list has no trailing zero because trailing zeros are explicitly deleted after each update. The target list consisting of \(n\) ones has zero extension \(Q_n\). Thus (18) implies in both directions
\[
 L_n(t)=[\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{n\text{ times}}]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E_n(t)=Q_n. \tag{19}
\]
For completeness, the reverse direction uses the absence of a trailing zero: if the zero extension equals \(Q_n\), the list cannot have length less than \(n\), because position \(n-1\) must contain one; it cannot have length greater than \(n\), because its last entry would then have to be zero, contradicting the absence of trailing zeros. Its length is therefore \(n\), and all entries are one.

By definition, \(a(n)\) is the least time at which the list reaches this all-one target. Equation (19) says that for every \(n\ge1\), this least time is exactly \(T_n\). Therefore (17) becomes
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+1
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 a(n+1)=a(n)+2

automatically for every integer \(n\ge1\). Equivalently,
\[
 a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
which is the conjectured finite-difference property.
